newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House banking bill to go to Rules panel Tues.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House banking bill to go to Rules panel Tues.

text.p: Banking legislation that has been stuck in a net of industry disagreement during this Congress will move a step closer to a vote on Tuesday when it goes before the U.S. House Rules Committee.
House Banking Committee Chairman James Leach, R-Iowa, introduced a bill on Monday that combined various elements into one piece of legislation.

Insurance agents supported the latest version, while bankers didn't oppose it in the hopes of moving the process forward and then later trying to shape legislation more favorably when the Senate and House hammer out differences in a Conference Committee.
If the bill gets through the Rules Committee, it is expected to go before the full House for a vote on Wednesday, a Banking Committee spokesman said.
The Senate was waiting to see the outcome in the House before moving forward on its version of banking legislation.
The House bill was aimed at reducing some regulatory burdens on banks, shoring up the fund that insures deposits at thrifts and modernizing the banking industry.
The bill also contained some insurance provisions that placated insurance agents who have fought to protect their turf from encroachment by banks.
In the version of the legislation now making its way through the House, bank holding companies would not be allowed to expand their operations further into insurance or annuities.

"It's a delicately balanced package, that has minimal but important insurance provisions, and we are able to support the bill," Phil Anderson, a lobbyist for the Independent Insurance Agents of America, said.
"As of right now, we would not oppose the Leach bill in order to have the process go forward," Ed Yingling, a lobbyist for the American Bankers Association, said.
The Rules Committee decides how a bill will be considered on the floor.
The Rules Committee can set the amount of time for debate and limit the number of amendments that can be offered.
Many Democrats on the House Banking Committee have objected to some provisions in the bill that they say would reduce consumer protections, and were expected to vote against the legislation.
Democrats sent the Rules Committee a "partial" list of 30 amendments they would like to see attached to the bill.
Industry representatives expect a close vote on the bill.
"I think it's going to be close, but I think the chairman's (Leach) going to get a bill through the House," Kenneth Guenther, a lobbyist for the Independent Bankers Association of America, said.
